methodological_rigor.justification: The study evaluates two pre-existing open-source AI models (EAGLE and DeepGEM) on two independent cohorts (DFCI n=1759 and TNM-I n=339) with paired NGS and H&E WSIs, plus TCGA for technical validation. Ancestry was inferred from germline data and stratified analyses were performed, with prevalence-matched subsampling to test whether mutation frequency drove subgroup differences. Limitations include ancestry data available only for one cohort, as acknowledged. The reported AUCs include 95% CIs derived from 1000 bootstrap resamples, supporting robust inference.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: External validation of AI pathology tools to triage EGFR testing has direct translational relevance given global gaps in biomarker testing access (>40% clinicians treating without results). The dual-threshold strategy yielding a 57% test reduction with sensitivity 0.84 and specificity 0.99 points to a practical triage workflow. As a retrospective multicohort validation of a prediction model, Oxford LoE 2b (cohort-level external validation) is appropriate.

reporting_quality.justification: The authors explicitly state adherence to TRIPOD-AI, appropriate for a prediction-model validation study. Primary outcome (AUC), 95% CIs, cohort characteristics, and subgroup analyses are reported, with eMethods and supplementary figures referenced. Models are described as open-source with references to their original codebases (EAGLE, DeepGEM). Data-sharing statements for DFCI/TNM-I patient-level data are not visible in the normalized text, and supplementary materials are referenced but not included.

novelty_literature.justification: The work provides one of the first large independent external validations of open-source pathology foundation models for EGFR prediction and specifically documents ancestry-associated performance variability (AUC drop to 0.68 in Asian ancestry) and tissue-context variability (pleural AUC 0.66). Prior reports had validated EAGLE/DeepGEM internally; the novelty lies in cross-institutional, ancestry-stratified, specimen-type-stratified evaluation. It is an extension rather than a first-in-class discovery but fills a documented fairness/generalizability gap.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with a logical structure: reproduction on TCGA, then DFCI, then TNM-I, then subgroup and thresholding analyses. Results are presented with explicit AUCs and CIs, and figures communicate overall and subgroup performance. The abstract and limitations are concise and the discussion links findings to clinical implications without overclaiming.

key_strengths: Large multicohort external validation (2098 patients) with paired NGS and H&E
Ancestry-stratified analysis with genetic ancestry inferred from germline data
Prevalence-matched subsampling supports that Asian subgroup drop is not explained by mutation frequency
Practical triage strategy demonstrated: 57% test reduction with sensitivity 0.84 and specificity 0.99
key_concerns: Ancestry data limited to the DFCI cohort
Small Asian subgroup (n=95) produces wide CIs and may limit inference
Patient-level data availability statement not visible in normalized text
Mechanistic explanation for ancestry-related morphologic shift remains speculative
chief_reviewer.rationale: Solid external validation with fairness analysis and a clinically actionable triage strategy; methodologically sound but incremental relative to original EAGLE/DeepGEM work, placing the paper comfortably at a Tier 2 venue such as JAMA Oncology or similar, with minor revisions to clarify data sharing and sample sizes.
